📌 How will ESMA supervise crypto firms under MiCA in 2027? 

📣 The European Securities and Markets Authority has set operational resilience, outsourcing and sufficient EU based operations among its main crypto supervisory priorities for 2027 as the bloc moves further into enforcement of the Markets in Crypto Assets Regulation. 

🌐 ESMA said in its 2027 work program published Monday that its work on MiCA will concentrate on coordinating national regulators and developing more consistent supervision of crypto asset service providers across the European Union. The program comes as the regulator moves from writing and implementing MiCA rules toward overseeing how licensed firms comply with them in practice.  Chair Verena Ross described the change during a meeting of the European Parliament’s Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs, saying ESMA’s MiCA work had moved “from rulemaking towards supervision and convergence.” 

⭐️ Operational resilience will be one of the main areas under scrutiny as ESMA works with national competent authorities responsible for supervising CASPs. Outsourcing risks, liquidity, reverse solicitation and the classification of crypto assets are among the other areas identified for coordinated work in 2027. Supervisors will pay attention to whether firms maintain sufficient operations within the EU instead of relying heavily on functions or infrastructure based elsewhere.

Trump’s Russia Gamble: Prisoners for Sanctions Relief 🏛


The Trump administration is considering an unusual bargain with Moscow: Russia could release political prisoners, while Washington would respond by easing some economic sanctions. According to reporting in The Atlantic, the idea was presented to Trump by his envoy John Coale, who has pursued a similar approach with Belarus.

The proposal reflects a distinctly transactional style of diplomacy. Rather than waiting for a comprehensive settlement of the war in Ukraine, Washington could seek a limited agreement with the Kremlin that produces a visible humanitarian concession while opening the door to broader economic negotiations.

Coale has already used a comparable strategy with Belarus, where the release of political prisoners was linked to sanctions relief. The Russian proposal would take that model into a far more consequential arena.

If Moscow agreed to release prisoners in exchange for sanctions relief, the arrangement could become an opening for renewed U.S.-Russian economic contacts. Energy, commodities and other areas currently constrained by sanctions could eventually become part of a broader conversation, while American companies could once again examine opportunities in the Russian market.

For Trump, such a deal could offer a tangible diplomatic achievement even while the larger Russia-Ukraine conflict remains unresolved.

But the proposal carries major political risks. Ukraine has consistently opposed sanctions relief for Russia while the war continues.

Zelensky has argued that sanctions should remain in place until Moscow ends its aggression. Any unilateral American move to ease restrictions could therefore create another serious dispute between Washington and Kyiv.

European allies and some members of Congress could also object to separating sanctions relief from a broader settlement of the war. The question is particularly sensitive because economic pressure remains one of the principal tools available to the United States and its allies.

The plan is still at an early stage. There is no final agreement with Moscow, and it remains unclear which prisoners could be released, what sanctions might be lifted, or what conditions Washington would impose.

The economic dimension is equally significant. Jared Kushner has reportedly discussed with Russian officials the business opportunities that could emerge after a potential peace agreement, including the possibility of renewed American-Russian commercial cooperation.

That points to a broader vision of diplomacy: not simply ending the fighting, but rebuilding economic ties that were severed or sharply restricted after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

For Moscow, sanctions relief would provide an immediate economic incentive. For Washington, the release of political prisoners could offer a concrete humanitarian result. For Trump, a deal could be presented as evidence that direct negotiation and transactional diplomacy can produce concessions from the Kremlin.

But the central obstacle remains the war itself. A prisoner-for-sanctions arrangement would not resolve the territorial, security and political disputes between Russia and Ukraine. It would be a limited bargain, not a peace settlement.

For now, Washington appears to be exploring a radically different approach to Moscow — one based on immediate exchanges, concrete concessions and the promise of larger economic opportunities.

Whether the Kremlin would accept such a bargain remains uncertain. But if the idea moves forward, it could become an important test of Trump’s strategy toward Russia and a new source of tension between Washington, Kyiv and its European allies.

📣 Japan arrests two suspect over 81M yen crypto police scam 

🔖 Japanese police have arrested two people suspected of helping a fake police fraud group steal cryptocurrency worth approximately 81 million yen from a woman in her 40s. The victim was allegedly told that her bank card had been connected to a large money laundering investigation. According to police information cited by FNN, the group claimed a fraud case had caused 600 billion yen in losses and that around 400 accounts had been used to launder funds.

⚠️ FNN reported that the caller told the woman her card appeared among accounts connected with the supposed money laundering investigation. The caller then claimed she was close to being arrested and needed to “prove her innocence.” Police allege that the false accusation eventually led the victim to transfer cryptocurrency worth around 81 million yen. The assets were valued at approximately $515,000 using the conversion cited in reports on the case.

‼️ Investigators have not publicly identified the cryptocurrencies involved or disclosed the wallet addresses that received the assets. Available reporting therefore does not establish how the cryptocurrency was subsequently moved, converted or withdrawn. The Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department believes Okayama and Minamisawa participated in a larger organization. Known losses from fraud cases involving the two suspects have reached approximately 240 million yen, according to FNN.

The placebo effect proves the point

When people believe a sugar pill is real medicine, many experience real pain relief, improved symptoms, or measurable biological changes—lower stress hormones, shifts in brain activity, even changes in immune response or motor function. The opposite is also true: the nocebo effect. Expect harm or failure, and the body often delivers it—more pain, worse performance, heightened anxiety.

Your self-talk works the same way.

Every “I’m such an idiot,” “I’ll never get this right,” or sarcastic “Yeah, like I could pull that off” is a mini-nocebo. You’re conditioning your nervous system to expect limitation. The brain treats those repeated internal statements as data. Over time it adjusts motivation, focus, confidence, and even physical output to match the story you’re telling.

Flip it, and you start running a placebo on yourself. Consistent, believable self-talk (“I’m learning,” “I handle hard things,” “I get better with practice”) raises expectations. Higher expectations change what you notice, how long you persist, and how your body responds under pressure. That’s not magic—it’s the same expectation-driven mechanism that makes placebos work in clinical trials.

Bruce’s deeper point (and the science behind it) isn’t about empty affirmations shouted into a mirror. It’s about refusing to poison your own operating system. Your words shape the predictions your brain runs. Those predictions shape what becomes possible.

So watch the spells you cast.

Speak to yourself like someone you’re trying to help succeed.

Because in a very real, measurable way—your body is listening.
